summary:
Arkansas stands under the United States national framework on travel documents and entry. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad; the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records.

Facilities access inside Arkansas is restricted by statute. A bathroom bill became law on 11 April 2023 as Act 619, making Arkansas the fourth state to restrict transgender students' use of school bathrooms matching their gender identity; the measure was amended and extended in 2025. The Movement Advancement Project equality map catalogues state bans on transgender people's use of public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity, and its February 2026 citations document cites HB 1156 as a 2023 K-12 facility ban extended in 2025. Nationally, that tally counts bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states, while 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban.

Care access for transgender minors is banned in Arkansas. In 2021 the state became the first in the country to prohibit gender-affirming healthcare for trans youth after the legislature overrode the governor's veto; critics called it the single most extreme anti-trans law to ever pass through a state legislature. A federal judge enjoined the law for irreparable harm to minors while litigation continued, and litigation over the 2021 care ban is ongoing. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states nationally, and federal measures constraining care include Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 and October 2025 proposed rules that would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18, several of which have been blocked or enjoined in court.

A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment places Arkansas in its "The Worst States" grouping for anti-trans law in effect, alongside Alabama, Iowa, Indiana, Louisiana, Mississippi, Ohio, Oklahoma, North Carolina, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, West Virginia and Wyoming. That tier sits one level below "Do Not Travel", which the assessment assigns to Florida, Idaho, Kansas and Texas; Idaho entered the tier after a felony bathroom ban carrying up to five years, partially court-blocked but in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists, and Kansas after a bounty-hunter civil-suit regime. Screening at US checkpoints also carries an outing risk: TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy, and several foreign governments issued advisories in 2025 about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules.
tangentialFactors:
The Movement Advancement Project catalogues facility bans state by state, so Arkansas's restriction is one entry in a wider national pattern rather than an isolated rule; the same catalogue records that a majority of states and several territories have no such ban.

The July 2026 risk assessment grades every state on anti-trans law in effect and groups Arkansas with fourteen other states in its second-highest tier. The tier above Arkansas, "Do Not Travel", holds four states: Florida, Idaho, Kansas and Texas, with Idaho's promotion following a felony bathroom ban of up to five years and Kansas's following a civil-suit regime that allows third-party enforcement.

Arkansas's 2021 care ban was the first of its kind nationally and was followed by bans in 26 further states, so the litigation path in Arkansas has been a reference point for litigation elsewhere. Federal measures in 2025 and 2026, including Executive Order 14187 and the proposed Medicaid reimbursement rules, have moved in the same direction as state restrictions, and several have been blocked or enjoined in court.

Passport and visa handling under Executive Order 14168 applies uniformly across the United States and does not vary by state; foreign advisories issued in April 2025 and adjusted entry guidelines reported in March 2025 concerned federal document and data rules rather than any single state's laws.
localsOnly:
Arkansas state law has permitted transgender people to amend birth certificates since 1981, a resident document access that predates most current state-level restrictions.

The 2021 gender-affirming care ban applies to minors resident in Arkansas and was enacted by legislative override of the governor's veto; a federal judge enjoined it pending litigation, and litigation continues.

The 2023 school facility restriction, as amended and extended in 2025, governs K-12 settings in Arkansas, with the Movement Advancement Project citing HB 1156 as the 2023 measure extended in 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources cite the 2023 Arkansas facility restriction under two different designations, Act 619 and HB 1156, and the inventory does not resolve whether these refer to the same measure or to distinct provisions.

The current scope and enforceability of the injunction against the 2021 care ban is not resolved in the inventory; the sources state only that a federal judge enjoined the law for irreparable harm while litigation continued and that litigation is ongoing.

No source in the inventory records enforcement of the Arkansas facility restriction against a visitor, an arrest under it, or an Arkansas-specific travel advisory, so the practical exposure for a trans visitor in state facilities is not established here.

The July 2026 assessment's tier definitions and methodology are described only at the level of grouping names; the criteria separating "The Worst States" from "Do Not Travel" are not set out in the inventory.
